title: Chapter 47
paragraphs: Mrs. Dashwood was moved by the defence of her former favourite. She was glad to see him cleared of some of the guilt attributed to him, felt sorry for him, and wished him happy. But the old feelings could not return. Nothing could restore him to Marianne with his promises unbroken and his character unstained. Nothing could erase the knowledge of what he had made her suffer, or remove his guilt towards Eliza. He could not regain Mrs. Dashwood's former esteem, therefore, or threaten Colonel Brandon's prospects.

Had Mrs. Dashwood heard Willoughby's account directly, as Elinor had, witnessed his distress, and felt the influence of his face and manner, she would probably have pitied him more. But Elinor could neither reproduce in her retelling the feelings first aroused in herself, nor wished to do so. Reflection had steadied her judgement and moderated her estimate of what Willoughby deserved. She therefore wanted to state only the plain truth, presenting the facts fairness to his character required, without tender embellishments to mislead the imagination.

That evening, when all three were together, Marianne voluntarily began to speak of him again. The effort was evident in the restless thoughtfulness that had occupied her for some time, in her rising colour as she spoke, and in her unsteady voice.
“I want to assure you both,” she said, “that I see everything as you would wish me to see it.”

Mrs. Dashwood would have interrupted at once with tender reassurance, but Elinor earnestly signalled her to remain silent. She wanted to hear Marianne's own uninfluenced judgement. Marianne slowly continued.

“What Elinor told me this morning is a great relief. I have now heard exactly what I wanted to hear.” Her voice failed for a few moments. Recovering, she added more calmly, “I am quite satisfied now. I wish nothing changed. I could never have been happy with him after learning all this, as sooner or later I must have done. I could have felt neither trust nor respect. Nothing could have removed it from my mind.”

“I know, I know!” her mother exclaimed. “Happy with a man who lived so immorally! Someone who so wounded the peace of our dearest friend, the best of men! No, my Marianne's heart could never find happiness with such a man. Her conscience, her sensitive conscience, would have felt everything her husband's ought to feel.”
Marianne sighed and said again, “I wish nothing changed.”

“You see it exactly as a good heart and sound judgement must,” Elinor said. “And I expect you understand, as I do, that this is not the only reason to believe your marriage would have brought many certain troubles and disappointments, with little support from a love on his side far less certain. If you had married, you would always have been poor. He admits his own extravagance. His whole conduct shows that self-denial is a word he scarcely understands. His demands and your inexperience, combined with a small, very small income, would have caused difficulties no _less_ painful because you had never known or imagined them before. Your own honour and honesty would, I know, have made you attempt every economy you could once you understood the situation. Perhaps, while your saving reduced only your own comforts, you would have been allowed to practise it. But beyond that—and how little could even your greatest efforts alone have done to halt a ruin begun before the marriage?—if you had reasonably tried to reduce _his_ pleasures, might you not have weakened his love instead of persuading such selfish feelings to agree? Might he not have regretted the marriage that brought him those difficulties?”
Marianne's lips trembled. “Selfish?” she repeated, in a tone that asked, “Do you really believe he is selfish?”

“His entire behaviour, from beginning to end, rested on selfishness,” Elinor answered. “It first made him play with your feelings. When he began to love you himself, it made him postpone admitting it. Finally, it took him away from Barton. In every action, his own enjoyment or comfort was the principle that governed him.”
“That is very true. _My_ happiness was never his purpose.”

“Now he regrets what he did,” Elinor continued. “Why? Because it has not worked out well for himself. It has not made him happy. His finances are secure; he suffers no trouble there. He thinks only that he has married a woman less sweet-tempered than you. But does that prove he would have been happy with you? The difficulties would have been different. He would have suffered the financial distress which, now it is removed, he counts as nothing. He could not have complained of his wife's temper, but would always have been short of money, always poor. Probably he would soon have considered the countless comforts of an unburdened estate and a good income far more important, even to happiness at home, than merely having a pleasant-tempered wife.”
“I don't doubt it,” Marianne said. “There is nothing for me to regret except my own foolishness.”
“Say rather your mother's lack of judgement, my child,” Mrs. Dashwood said. “_She_ must take the blame.”

Marianne would not let her continue. Satisfied that each recognised her own mistake, Elinor wanted to avoid dwelling on the past in ways that might weaken her sister's spirits. She therefore immediately returned to their first subject.

“I think _one_ conclusion can fairly be drawn from the whole story: every difficulty Willoughby has suffered began with his first wrongdoing, his treatment of Eliza Williams. That offence was the source of every lesser one and of all his present unhappiness.”

Marianne agreed with deep feeling. Her mother took the remark as an opportunity to list Colonel Brandon's sufferings and merits with all the warmth friendship and purpose could jointly inspire. Marianne, however, did not seem to hear much of it.

As Elinor had expected, during the next two or three days Marianne no longer gained strength as quickly. But her determination remained firm and she still tried to appear cheerful and at ease. Her sister could therefore safely trust time to restore her health.

Margaret returned, reuniting the whole family in the quiet of the cottage. If they did not pursue their usual studies with quite the energy of their first days at Barton, they at least planned to pursue them energetically in future.

Elinor became impatient for news of Edward. Since leaving London, she had heard nothing of him, no fresh plans, not even certain information about where he was living. Marianne's illness had occasioned several letters between Elinor and John. His first included this sentence: “We know nothing of our unfortunate Edward, and cannot inquire about so forbidden a subject, but assume he is still at Oxford.” That was all the correspondence told her. The later letters did not even mention his name. She would not, however, remain ignorant of his actions for long.
One morning their manservant was sent to Exeter on business. Later, while waiting at table, he answered his mistress's questions about the result of his errand, then volunteered this information.
“I suppose you know, ma'am, that Mr. Ferrars has got married.”

Marianne started violently and fixed her eyes on Elinor. Seeing her turn pale, she fell back in her chair in a fit of distress. As Mrs. Dashwood answered the servant, her own eyes had instinctively turned the same way. Elinor's expression shocked her by revealing the depth of her suffering. A moment later, equally distressed by Marianne's condition, she did not know which daughter needed her most.

The servant noticed only that Miss Marianne had become unwell. Sensibly, he called a maid, who helped Mrs. Dashwood support her into the next room. Marianne was somewhat better by then. Leaving her with Margaret and the maid, their mother returned to Elinor. Still deeply shaken, she had recovered enough reason and voice to begin asking Thomas where he had obtained the news. Mrs. Dashwood immediately took over the questioning, letting Elinor hear the information without the effort of asking for it.
“Who told you Mr. Ferrars had married, Thomas?”

“I saw him myself this morning in Exeter, ma'am, and his wife too, Miss Steele as was. They were stopped in a chaise outside the New London Inn. I went there with a message from Sally at the Park to her brother, one of the post-boys. As I passed the carriage, I looked up and recognised the younger Miss Steele straight away. I took off my hat. She knew me, called me over, and asked after you and the young ladies, especially Miss Marianne. She told me to give you her compliments and Mr. Ferrars's, their best compliments and respects. They were sorry not to have time to come and see you, but they had to hurry on. They were going further down the country for a little while. When they came back, though, they would be sure to visit.”
“But did she say that she was married, Thomas?”

“Yes, ma'am. She smiled and said she'd changed her name since she was last in these parts. She was always a friendly, freely spoken young lady, with very civil manners. So I took the liberty of congratulating her.”
“Was Mr. Ferrars there in the carriage with her?”
“Yes, ma'am. I just saw him leaning back inside, but he didn't look up. He was never a gentleman who talked a great deal.”
Elinor's heart readily explained why he had not come forward. Her mother probably found the same explanation.
“Was anybody else travelling in the carriage?”
“No, ma'am. Only the two of them.”
“Do you know where they had come from?”
“Straight from London, so Miss Lucy—Mrs. Ferrars—told me herself.”
“And are they travelling further west?”
“Yes, ma'am, but not for long. They'll soon be coming back, and then they'll be certain to call here.”

Mrs. Dashwood looked at Elinor, who knew better than to expect them. The message was entirely characteristic of Lucy, and she felt certain Edward would never come near them. Quietly, she told her mother that they were probably going to Mr. Pratt's, near Plymouth.
Thomas appeared to have finished his news. Elinor looked as though she wanted more.
“Did you see them leave before you came away?”
“No, ma'am. The horses were just being brought out, but I couldn't wait any longer. I was afraid I would be late.”
“Did Mrs. Ferrars seem well?”
“Yes, ma'am. She said she was very well. I've always thought her a very pretty young lady, and she seemed extremely contented.”

Mrs. Dashwood could think of nothing else to ask. Thomas and the tablecloth, equally unnecessary now, were soon dismissed. Marianne had already sent word that she would eat no more. Her mother and Elinor had lost their appetites too. Margaret might consider herself fortunate that, through all the distress her sisters had lately suffered and all their frequent reasons to neglect meals, she had never before been obliged to miss her dinner.

After dessert and wine were set out, Mrs. Dashwood and Elinor were left alone. For a long time they sat together in matching thoughtfulness and silence. Their mother dared risk no remark and offered no consolation. She now realised her mistake in trusting Elinor's account of her feelings. Rightly, she concluded that her daughter had deliberately softened everything to spare her additional distress while she was suffering for Marianne. Elinor's careful consideration had misled her into believing that the attachment she had once understood so well was much slighter than she formerly thought, or than it now proved to be. She feared that this belief had made her unfair, inattentive, even almost unkind to Elinor. Marianne's more openly expressed and immediately visible sorrow had absorbed too much of her tenderness. She had forgotten that her other daughter might suffer nearly as much, certainly with less responsibility for it and greater courage.
